newsitem.title: HAITI: Haitian labor advocates applaud sweatshop accord.
newsitem.headline: Haitian labor advocates applaud sweatshop accord.

text.p: Haitian labour advocates on Monday applauded an apparel industry agreement barring the use of child labour and other sweatshop conditions at shoe and clothing factories used by U.S. firms.
U.S. President Bill Clinton endorsed the code of conduct at a White House ceremony on Monday, saying it would help improve the lives of millions of garment workers worldwide.
The code of conduct set a maximum mandatory work week of 48 hours plus 12 hours of mandatory overtime, with at least one day off in every seven-day period.

Advocates for workers in the lowest paying market in the hemisphere said they hoped the agreement would change the conditions in which Haitian labourers work, putting in long hours in huge factories with small windows in the capital's industrial park.

"The workers in Haiti under this agreement will have the right to organise, unionize and bargain collectively," said Charles Kernaghan, executive director of the New York-based National Labour Committee. "That will send a shiver up the spine of factory owners in Haiti."

The National Labour Committee has led an ongoing high profile "Mickey is a Rat" campaign against companies paying workers only 33 cents an hour to manufacture Walt Disney Co clothing in Haiti -- a wage that workers say they cannot support themselves on.

"I work all day, I take the bus, I eat very little, and I have almost nothing to take home to my hungry family or to send my kids to school," one Haitian worker at a factory sewing Disney clothes recently told Reuters under condition of anonymity.

The pact requires apparel companies and subcontractors to pay at least the minimum wage or prevailing industry wage, and bars companies from employing children under the age of 15, or 14 in countries that permit it.

Workers' advocates contend the factories can afford to make some concessions. Haitian apparel exports to the United States were up 36 percent to $98 million last year over 1995, according to the American Apparel Manufacturers Association.
